figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: RoboTryOn pipeline. (a) The image model sequentially translates keyframes of a human video into robot keyframes, the video model synthesizes the motion between them under the guidance of the hand skeleton flow, and the inverse dynamics model labels the actions. (b) The image model inpaints the masked human frame, using the previous robot keyframe as a reference. (c) The video model synthesizes the robot video, conditioned on the robot keyframes at their temporal positions and the skeleton flow.
figures.headline: The pipeline translates human keyframes into robot keyframes, interpolates robot video between them, and labels actions from that video.
citing_sentences: Given $\mathbf{X}^{h}$ and a reference image of the target robot $r$, RoboTryOn uses a three-stage pipeline to generate a robot demonstration $\hat{\mathbf{X}}^{r}=\big((\hat{\mathbf{o}}^{r}_{t},\hat{\mathbf{q}}_{t},\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{t})_{t=1}^{T},{\mathbf{c}}\big)$ that follows the human motion (see Figure 1).

The image generation model $f_{\theta}$ aims to translate a human keyframe into a robot keyframe as inpainting guided by a reference image: it fills the masked region $\mathbf{M}_{t}$ with the target robot in the pose specified by the skeleton $\mathbf{S}_{t}$, using the reference image to determine its appearance (see Figure 1(b)).

The video generation model $g_{\phi}$ interpolates between the translated keyframes $\hat{\mathbf{o}}^{r}_{\mathcal{T}}=(\hat{\mathbf{o}}^{r}_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{T}}$ to synthesize the full robot video, guided by the hand skeleton flow $\mathbf{S}_{1:T}=(\mathbf{S}_{t})_{t=1}^{T}$ (see Figure 1(c)).

To evaluate action labels without ground truth robot actions, we replay them open loop in a simulated replica of each scene and measure task completion (see Figure 4a).

Replay succeeds in 69.7% of episodes with our labels and 34.8% with retargeted labels (see Figure 4c), and the difference arises mainly during grasping: retargeted motions bring the robot hand near the object, but imprecise hand reconstruction and the difference in hand geometry prevent a secure grasp (see Figure 4b).

abstract: Robot foundation models have shown remarkable performance in robot control, yet adapting them to a new task still relies heavily on teleoperated demonstrations. Egocentric human videos offer a scalable substitute, but overlaying rendered robots on human videos or retargeting human poses into robot actions leaves significant visual or action gaps for high-DoF robot embodiments. To address this limitation, we propose RoboTryOn, which treats human-to-robot translation as virtual try-on: try-on keeps the person and swaps the garment, RoboTryOn keeps the demonstrated motion and swaps the human for the robot. Specifically, RoboTryOn converts a human video into a video of the target robot specified by a reference image, while preserving the original task, objects, and background. To maintain visual consistency, we translate selected keyframes autoregressively and use them to guide video synthesis with motion conditioned on the human hand skeleton. Additionally, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) that incorporates depth features to infer action labels from synthesized videos for policy learning. Our experiments across multiple humanoid embodiments show that policies trained with our synthetic data improve the average success rate on novel tasks, including challenging bimanual manipulation, from 2% to 60%, without any real robot demonstration of those tasks. Moreover, training with our synthetic data matches the performance of policies trained solely on teleoperated demonstrations at approximately a third of the collection cost, demonstrating the cost efficiency of our approach.

sections.body: Robot foundation models still need teleoperated demonstrations for each new task, and collecting them is costly, especially for dexterous hands. Human videos are cheaper but differ from robot data in appearance, since a human arm and hand appear where the policy sees a robot. They also differ in action: hand reconstructions are imprecise, and retargeting reproduces the shape of the hand but not how firmly the robot must grip. RoboTryOn converts a human video into a paired robot demonstration with action labels. It generates a target robot video that keeps the task and scene, then predicts joint-space actions with an inverse dynamics model. Averaged over two robot embodiments, success on out-of-domain tasks rises from 2.1% to 60.0%. Training with synthetic data matches teleoperated training at approximately a third of the collection cost.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Human videos differ from robot demonstrations in appearance and action, and RoboTryOn is proposed to translate them.

sections.body: This section groups related work into three lines. The first covers learning from human videos through visual representations, retargeting, rendering, and simulation. The second covers generative human-to-robot translation. The authors state that Mitty learns from paired human and robot data, including synthetic rendered pairs, and that H2R-Grounder removes the need for paired supervision. The third covers video synthesis with action labeling. The authors state that their approach supports multiple dexterous embodiments through shared generative models and produces demonstrations with action labels. For keyframe-based generation they adopt the decomposition used in DreamVVT, and for action inference they follow prior work that uses inverse dynamics models.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior human-video methods retarget, render, or translate footage, while this work adds action labels for policy learning.

sections.body: The method has three stages. An image model inpaints the masked human arm and hand with the target robot, posed by a two-dimensional hand skeleton and styled by a reference image. Keyframes are chosen at local minima of wrist speed, and each keyframe is translated conditioned on the previous translated robot keyframe. A video model then interpolates the robot motion between keyframes under the skeleton flow. An inverse dynamics model predicts joint-space action chunks from frames 20 steps apart. Inverse kinematics then corrects the wrist position, because the model estimates wrist position less accurately than hand reconstruction does. The policy is trained on the synthetic demonstrations alone or together with teleoperated data.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: A three-stage pipeline translates human keyframes into robot keyframes, synthesizes robot video, and labels actions with an inverse dynamics model.

sections.body: Experiments use two bimanual robots with dexterous hands, OpenArm and RB-Y1, on eleven tabletop tasks. Four in-domain pick-and-place tasks have 50 teleoperated demonstrations per robot. Seven out-of-domain tasks have only human videos, covering a new object, a new goal, two new skills, and three bimanual tasks. The baselines EgoMimic and Masquerade both retarget the hand and differ in how they edit the human arm, and both apply the same edit at test time. Each policy is evaluated over 28 trials per task. On OpenArm, in-domain success rises from 47.3% to 75.9% when synthetic data is added. Both baselines largely fail on out-of-domain tasks, with success rates below 10%. On RB-Y1, out-of-domain success rises from 1.0% to 46.9%.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Adding synthetic demonstrations to teleoperated ones raised OpenArm out-of-domain success from 3.1% to 73.0%.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the method. RoboTryOn translates human keyframes into robot keyframes, synthesizes the robot video between them under hand skeleton guidance, and labels its actions with an inverse dynamics model. The authors report that on two real robots with dexterous hands, the synthesized demonstrations teach a policy seven tasks with no robot demonstration of those tasks, including bimanual ones. They also report that translated human video matches the success rate of teleoperated demonstrations at about a third of their collection cost. The authors refer the reader to Appendix A for limitations and future work.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Synthesized demonstrations teach seven tasks without robot demonstrations, matching teleoperation at about a third of its cost.

sections.body: The limitations section states that each new robot needs a few hours of teleoperated video to train the generative models and the inverse dynamics model, and that actions are pseudo labels that cannot capture forces. It also states that the wrist correction depends on head camera calibration, that a moving camera falls outside the training distribution, and that demonstrated motions must be executable by the robot. Evaluation covers tabletop manipulation on two robots, and the GR-1 could not be evaluated. Future work proposes scaling to large egocentric corpora and improving the inverse dynamics model with policy rollouts. Implementation details, per-task tables, and figure captions follow.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists limitations and future work, implementation details, per-task results, and figure captions for the experiments.
